source.title: Inoculation Adapters Improve Upon Inoculation Prompting

record.file_problem: This is a LessWrong link-post summary of a preprint, not the preprint's full text. Numerical values and model names are not provided in the post.
record.tranche_reason: Reports results on mitigating undesired-trait generalization with inoculation prompting and adapters, using a method and setup that differ from the original narrow-task fine-tuning claim.
record.gate_note: The post reports qualitative outcomes for inoculation methods and undesired-trait generalization, including surprising-backdoor probes. It mentions figures and confidence intervals but supplies no plotted values. Do not infer numerical results from those references. The post's statement that direct requests for undesired traits can elicit stronger expression is excluded as a result for these versions because the behavior is deliberately elicited.
record.test_reason: The study's main subject is a new mitigation, inoculation adapters. It also reports, for inoculation prompting (IP), that IP leaves strong contextual-trigger backdoors of the undesired trait across 3 setups. That bears on whether framing-based inoculation prevents emergent misalignment (V6), and suggests the prevention is partial. The text is a link-post summary with no numbers.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add these points: the authors claim IA suppresses undesired traits (including EM) more strongly than IP. All IA variants are less prone to trigger backdoors than IP, which leaves strong ones. Vanilla IA retains desired traits worse than the baselines, which GIA and CGIA fix at some cost to trigger robustness.
record.recipe_differences: The post describes a three-stage inoculation-adapter method: train a LoRA on undesired-trait examples, freeze it while training a task LoRA (optionally with gates), then deploy without the inoculation adapter. It also compares inoculation prompting; this is not the original narrow insecure-code fine-tuning recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Results are strongly setup-dependent. Backdoor outcomes differ across IA, GIA, CGIA, and IP; the post notes three of nine setups were designed to be hard for inoculation prompting.

fits_no_version.finding: Inoculation adapters (a frozen LoRA carrying the undesired trait during task training) suppress undesired-trait generalization, including EM, more on average than IP, preventative steering and CAFT. Vanilla IA shows no detectable trigger backdoors beyond No FT / SFT(Safe), while GIA and CGIA show some. The setup dependence is strong and the confidence intervals are wide.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training with a frozen adapter implementing the undesired trait, then removing it, prevents emergent misalignment with fewer hidden triggered backdoors than inoculation prompting.

record.problems: This post is a summary rather than the full preprint and omits numerical values, model names, model sizes, and setup-level results. It reports wide confidence intervals and substantial setup dependence. The post also does not provide seed or coherence-filter results.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for desired-trait retention because the versions do not name that measure. Direct-request expression is omitted because the behavior is deliberately elicited. The post mentions best-of-three choices and a best-of-ten prompt selection but provides no outcome values for those choices.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tune or secure-code / class-request controls are described.
There are four EM setups 'from three sources', but the datasets are not named and no per-dataset results are given.
No RL; the authors say IA's impact on RL is unstudied.
No shared-direction or persona mechanism is tested.
Brief benign re-training is not tested. IP's plain-evaluation suppression of EM relative to an un-inoculated fine-tune is not reported numerically in the post.
Effect size, seeds, coherence filters, training timing and model sizes are all absent.

missing.what: EM-setup undesired-trait scores for IP vs plain SFT (no inoculation) at standard evaluation, needed to judge whether inoculation prevents EM
missing.locator: Detailed results figure with 95% bootstrap CIs; preprint arXiv:2606.30252

missing.what: Trigger-probe backdoor strengths for IP per setup and per prompt category, with model names
IP performance in the 3 setups designed to be hard for IP (new capability, non-instruct model, hard-to-elicit trait)
missing.locator: Effectiveness on hard-to-elicit traits section; preprint

record.verdict_notes: This is a link-post summary of the preprint, with no numbers or model names, so all states are qualitative. IA is treated as a distinct mitigation rather than V6's 'framing as requested', so the IA rows are moved to fits_no_version. The post's design rationale says IP struggles with hard-to-elicit traits and non-instruct models. No IP result for those settings is quoted, so it is not used as a verdict.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning or matched secure-code and class-request controls are described.
The post mentions several undesired traits but does not identify or report results for the specified medical, financial, reward-hack, or number-sequence fine-tunes.
The post says the impact of inoculation adapters on RL training has not been studied.
No shared linear direction or persona-feature mechanism is tested.
The post reports inoculation prompting and inoculation adapters, but not brief benign retraining.
The post gives no model names or sizes and does not report seed robustness, coherence-filter results, or when during training the effect appears.

rows.subject: five model families (aggregate; names not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Train task adapters with inoculation adapters, including gated variants, to limit undesired-trait generalization.
rows.baseline: Other baselines, including preventative steering and concept-ablation fine-tuning; exact values not stated
rows.value: On average, inoculation adapters suppress undesired-trait generalization better than the other baselines.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals for normalized performance aggregated across the nine setups are described as wide; numeric intervals not stated.
rows.locator: Post text accompanying the selective-generalization figures
rows.note: The post describes an aggregate across nine setups and five model families; it does not give model-level results or numerical values.
rows.check: This compares the study's own method (IA) with other baselines. It aggregates nine setups, only four of which are emergent misalignment. IA trains a trait-carrying LoRA rather than framing the behaviour as requested, so it does not measure what V6 names. V7 is not measured either: no effect size, seeds, coherence filtering or training timing.

rows.subject: five model families (aggregate; names not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Use inoculation prompting during training to elicit the undesired trait, then evaluate without that prompt.

conditions.value: four emergent-misalignment setups out of nine

rows.value: Across three probed setups, inoculation prompting introduced several strong surprising backdoors triggered by prompts related to the inoculation prompt and task domain.
rows.note: The post describes trigger-probe outcomes qualitatively, without rates.
rows.check: The link to V6 is correct. IP appears to suppress the trait at plain evaluation but leaves strong backdoors triggered by inoculation-related and task-domain prompts. Baseline is No FT / SFT(Safe), not 'not stated'. The condition 'four EM setups' is wrong: the probes cover 3 setups, and the post does not say all are EM.

relation.reason: The post reports its own comparisons of undesired-trait expression under mitigation and contextual-trigger probes.

tranche.reason: The contextual-trigger results qualify V6: prompting-based inoculation can leave strong backdoors despite apparent suppression.

source_check.notes: This link post reports qualitative backdoor outcomes; the detailed setup identifiers and trigger categories cannot be checked from its text. Aggregate comparisons have wide confidence intervals and strong setup dependence.

statements.correction: Across three setups, IP introduces strong backdoors related to the inoculation prompt and task domain. CGIA improves desired-trait retention but introduces more backdoors than vanilla IA, weaker than IP. For four EM setups, IP(Best) selects among three prompts; one was selected as best-eliciting among ten generated prompts. Exact backdoor rates and setup identifiers are not stated.
statements.problem: The text supports contextual backdoors and a retention/robustness tradeoff, but supplies none of the named setup identifiers, specific trigger categories, failed-prompt examples, or villain-prompt selection details.
